A Judge Agent Closes the Reliability Gap
in AI-Generated Scientific Simulation
Chengshuai Yang
NextGen PlatformAI C Corp, USA
Correspondence: integrityyang@gmail.com
March 2026
Abstract.Large language models can generate scientific simulation code, but the generated code
silently fails on most non-textbook problems. We show that classical mathematical validation—
well-posedness, convergence, and error certification—can be fully automated by a Judge Agent,
reducing the silent-failure rate from 42% to 1.5% across 134 test cases spanning 12 scientific
domains. The headline result comes from a prospective benchmark: 72 blinded tasks submitted
by 12 independent scientists yield an 89% success rate (95% CI: [80%, 95%]) with automated error
bounds, versus 53% without the Judge. On clinical CT (the only powered experiment, n= 200),
the pipeline reaches 99% of expert quality. The residual 1.5% concentrates at bifurcation points
where certifiability breaks down. We formalize this boundary through thesimulability class S
and introduce spec.md, a structured specification format that makes any scientific computation
problem machine-readable and solver-independent. Code, data, and all 72 benchmark tasks are
publicly archived.
Classical mathematical validation—well-posedness, convergence, error bounds—can
be fully automated. A Judge Agent applying these checks to AI-generated simulation
code reduces silent failures from 42% to 1.5% across 134 test cases (12 domains). A
prospective benchmark of 72 blinded tasks from 12 independent scientists confirms
generalization: 89% success rate (95% CI: [80%, 95%]) with certified error bounds
versus 53% without the Judge. The residual 1.5% concentrates at bifurcation points,
formalizable as the boundary of the simulability classS.
Consider a plausible scenario: a researcher uses an LLM to generate a finite-element solver for
thermal stress in a reactor component. The code compiles, converges, and produces smooth
temperature fields—but a CFL violation in the time integrator means the stress predictions
are wrong by a factor of three. The error is caught only when a colleague runs an independent
simulation weeks later. Such silent failures are not hypothetical: in the SciCode benchmark [ 2],
frontier LLMs solve fewer than half of research-level computational problems correctly. The
wrong answers look as plausible as the right ones.
The silent-failure problem will deepen as LLM-generated code proliferates. Physics-informed
neural networks [ 1,3] learn solutions but provide no error certificates. Automated code generation
from variational forms (FEniCS [ 4], Firedrake [ 5]) is rigorous but requires expert formulation.
LLM-based scientific agents [ 6,7] generate protocols but do not address numerical convergence.
The reproducibility crisis [8, 44] needs a validation layer, not more code generators.
The mathematical tools for catching these failures already exist—Lax–Richtmyer convergence
theory [9], Hadamard well-posedness [ 10], CFL stability conditions [ 27]—but applying them
requires numerical analysis expertise that the typical end-user lacks. What has been missing is
(i) a formal characterization ofwhichproblems can be solved with bounded error by an automated
pipeline, and (ii) a system thatautomaticallyverifies this characterization and applies classical
checks to AI-generated simulation code.
We address both gaps with three interlocking contributions that form a hierarchy, not a list:

The foundation: thesimulability class S(Definition 1), which formalizes “what can be solved
reliably by any computational system” through four implementation-independent conditions—
finite specifiability (S1), Hadamard stability (S2), approximability (S3), and certifiability (S4).
Problems in Scan be solved with a user-specified error tolerance; problems outside S—at what
we call thescientific event horizon—cannot be guaranteed by any automated pipeline. The
pipeline’s successes and failures are not accidents; they are predicted by this formal theory.
The mechanism: a Judge Agent ( AJ) that automates verification of S2–S4 on AI-generated
code. Within a three-agent pipeline (Fig. 1), a Plan Agent ( AP) translates natural language
into a structured specification, AJvalidates S-membership via 5 pre-execution gates, and an
Execute Agent (AE) generates and runs the solver. After execution, AJcertifies the result (S4).
Removing the Judge increases the silent-failure rate from 1.5% to 42% across 134 test cases—the
headline empirical result.
The interface: spec.md, a structured specification format that realizes S1. Every problem in
Scan be expressed as a valid spec.md file encoding the six-tuple(Ω ,E,B,I,O,ε )—domain,
equations, boundary conditions, initial conditions, observables, and tolerance. The format is
solver-independent: any compliant solver can consume a spec.md file and any Judge can verify it.
The 72 prospective tasks are archived in this format, enabling independent replication without
access to our specific pipeline.
The underlying mathematics is entirely classical; the contribution is empirical evidence that
automated S-verification substantially reduces silent failures across 12 scientific domains, with a
median setup-time efficiency gain ofρ≈480×relative to expert workflows.
What this paper does not claim.This is not about building a better PDE solver: on any
single well-defined problem, COMSOL [ 11] or FEniCS will produce a more accurate solution
(Extended Data Table 5). It is not about LLM capabilities: the Judge works regardless of which
LLM generates the code. It is not about the 12 computational primitivesper se: they are an
engineering realization (Proposition 3), not the core contribution. And it is not a completed
theory of simulability: the completeness conjecture (Conjecture 4) is stated as a research direction,
not a proven result. The error bound is conditional on a correct spec.md specification; since
this specification is generated by an LLM, the pipeline’s end-to-end reliability depends on the
Judge’s ability to catch specification errors (Methods). The pipeline retains a 1.5% qualitative
failure rate at the boundary ofS(“Failure analysis,” below).

Results
The evidence presented below has three tiers of statistical strength, reported transparently:
1.Powered validation: clinical CT reconstruction ( n= 200), with bootstrap confidence
intervals.
2.Prospective benchmark: 72 blinded tasks from 12 independent scientists, with Clopper–
Pearson exact binomial CIs. Independently coordinated, protocol-locked before execution.
3.Feasibility case studies: seismic FWI ( n= 5), combustion ( n= 15), and 7 additional
domains reported in supplementary material. These demonstrate breadth, not statistical
inference.
All three tiers are complemented by 50 adversarial boundary probes that characterize the residual
1.5% failure rate.
The simulability class and its boundary
The Judge Agent’s checks are grounded in a formal characterization of which problems can be
solved with bounded error by an automated pipeline.
Definition 1(Simulability class S).A scientific computation problem Pbelongs to the simula-
bility classSif it satisfies four conditions:
(S1)Finite specifiability. Padmits a finite representation S= (Ω,E,B,I,O,ε ), whereΩis the
computational domain, Ethe governing equations, Bthe boundary conditions, Ithe initial
conditions,Othe observable (output functional), and εthe target tolerance. Each component
is encodable in a finite string over a standard alphabet.
(S2)Hadamard stability.The map F:D→X from problem data to solution is well-posed: the
solution exists, is unique within the specified function space, and depends continuously on the

data with a computable modulus of continuity.
(S3)Approximability.There exists a convergent discretization scheme—a sequence of finite-
dimensional problems Phparameterized by resolution h—such that∥Fh(D)−F(D)∥→ 0as
h→0, with a computable convergence rateq>0.
(S4)Certifiability.There exists a computable procedure that, given the approximation ˆx=Fh(D)
and the problem data D, produces a verified upper bound Bsatisfying∥ˆx−F(D)∥≤B≤ε ,
in finite time.
The six components of the specification tupleSare:
ΩComputational domain.The geometric or topological space on which the problem is
posed. Examples: a128 ×128pixel grid for CT imaging, a 2D channel with a backward-
facing step ( x∈[−5h,30h],y∈[−h, h ]) for turbulent flow, or a radial domain r∈[0,50a0]
for atomic structure. The domain specification includes dimensionality, coordinate system,
discretization geometry (structured grid, unstructured mesh, spectral basis), and characteristic
length scales.
EGoverning equations.The mathematical model relating unknowns to data. These may
be PDEs (Navier–Stokes, Schrödinger), integral equations (Radon transform in CT, Fredholm
equations in remote sensing), or algebraic systems (linear mixing models in hyperspectral
imaging). The specification includes all physical parameters (Reynolds number, regularization
weights, physical constants) and their numerical values.
BBoundaryconditions.Constraintsonthesolutionatthedomainboundaryoratinterfaces.
Examples: no-slip walls (u= 0) in fluid dynamics, non-negativity constraints ( xi,j≥0) in
tomographic reconstruction, or asymptotic decay ( ψ→ 0asr→∞) in quantum mechanics.
Includes the type (Dirichlet, Neumann, Robin, periodic) and values at each boundary segment.
IInitial conditions.The starting state for time-dependent problems or the initial guess for
iterative solvers. Examples: a filtered back-projection warm start for iterative CT reconstruc-
tion, a fully-developed turbulent inlet profile for channel flow simulation, or a hydrogen-like
orbital for Hartree–Fock iteration. For steady-state or inverse problems, Ispecifies the initial
iterate and any warm-start strategy.
OObservables.The output functionals—what is to be computed from the solution, and in
what form. These are rarely the full solution field; instead they are derived quantities such
as PSNR and SSIM for image reconstruction, reattachment length ( xr/h) and skin-friction
coefficient for fluid simulations, or ground-state energy for quantum systems. The observable
specification makes the acceptance criterion unambiguous.
εTarget tolerance.The quantitative accuracy threshold that defines success. Examples:
PSNR≥30dB for CT reconstruction, relative error ≤5%on mean velocity profiles for
turbulent flow, or energy error ≤1mHa for quantum chemistry. The tolerance is stated with
respect to a named metric and, where applicable, a reference solution or experimental dataset.
Together, these six fields make every problem machine-readable and self-contained: given a valid
S, any compliant solver can attempt the problem and any Judge can verify the result, without
ambiguity about what was asked or what counts as correct. All 72 prospective benchmark tasks
and 12 development problems are archived asspec.mdfiles encoding this tuple (Figure 2).
Condition S4 is the key distinction. A problem can becomputable(you can approximate the
solution) without beingcertifiable(you can prove your approximation is good enough). This
separation is what makes the Judge Agent necessary in principle, not just in practice: it is the
automated realization of S4.

Theboundary ∂SistheregimewhereatleastoneconditionofDefinition1fails—typicallybecause
S2 (well-posedness) degrades near a bifurcation or S4 (certifiability) fails as the error bound
diverges—and no automated pipeline can provide guarantees. We use the metaphor “scientific
event horizon” sparingly for this boundary, to emphasize that it represents afundamental limit
on certifiable simulation, not a limitation of a particular pipeline. Problems near ∂S(e.g.,
symmetry-breaking near a critical load, branch selection near a critical Reynolds number) are
where the pipeline’s residual 1.5% failures concentrate (“Failure analysis,” below).
The Judge Agent closes the reliability gap
To isolate the Judge’s contribution, we ran five conditions on 12 development problems (Extended
Data Table 4) and extended the comparison to 72 held-out tasks from external scientists (Fig. 3).
Without the Judge, the pipeline produces wrong answers on 42% of development problems and
47% of prospective tasks. The failures concentrate on non-textbook problems: stiff ODEs, inverse
problems, turbulent flows, and near-critical parameter regimes—precisely the problems near ∂S
where S2 or S4 are close to failing. With the Judge verifying S1–S4 membership in S, the success
rate is 100% on the 12 development problems (which were used to design the Judge’s checks) and
89% (64/72) on the held-out tasks (95% CI: [80%, 95%], Clopper–Pearson exact binomial [ 23]),
with automated error bounds (S4) on every successful solution. No other condition produces any
error bound.

discretization converges at O(h2)(S3), and the Morozov discrepancy principle [ 30] provides a
computable error bound (S4).

Failure analysis: probing∂S
We submitted 50 adversarial inputs specifically designed to probe ∂S, yielding 134 total test
cases with the 12 development and 72 prospective problems (Supplementary Table S3). We
note that 50 adversarial inputs is a limited probe; a larger adversarial suite ( n≥100) would
strengthen confidence in the 1.5% failure rate estimate.
APmisspecification(20 adversarial): incorrect equations in 4/20 (20%). AJcaught all 4
via dimensional inconsistency or non-physical parameters—failures in S1 (finite specifiability:
thespec.md did not correctly encode the problem). Three corrected after redesign, 1 required
human clarification.
AJfalse negatives(20 adversarial): incorrectly accepted 2/20 (10%) with condition numbers
>1012, indicating near-violation of S4 (certifiability: the error bound degrades as condition
number diverges). One caught by AEa posteriori; one produced volumetric locking ( ν= 0.4999
elasticity) that the quality audit flagged.
Qualitative failures(10 adversarial): 3/10 met the L2error bound but exhibited non-physical
artifacts (oscillations, missed symmetry-breaking, wrong shock structure). These are problems
that formally satisfy S1–S3 but where S4 (certifiability) is fragile: the error bound holds locally
but the Lipschitz constant grows sharply near the bifurcation point. Without the quality audit,
the silent-failure rate across all 134 problems is 6%. With the quality audit: 1.5% (2/134).

a result thatlookscorrect but fails the domain-specific tolerance when checked against
the expert baseline. The user receives no warning. Failures include wrong equations (S1),

Discussion
This paper makes one claim: automated mathematical validation—the Judge Agent, grounded
in the simulability class S—substantially narrows the reliability gap in AI-generated scientific
simulation. The evidence: removing the Judge increases the silent-failure rate from 1.5% to

Design implications: from validation to protocol.The CT QC extension above illustrates
a broader design principle: the six-tuple, the Judge’s S1–S4 verification, and the immutable
audit record together form a minimaltrust kernel—a small, stable nucleus around which new
scientific domains can dock without mutating the core. A new domain becomes compatible
when its benchmarkable tasks admit a finite spec.md representation, at least one executable
realization (solver, workflow, or deterministic pipeline), and a post-execution certificate tied to
explicit acceptance criteria. Crucially, simulation is not required: the CT QC case shows that
deterministic measurement-validation pipelines are sufficient wherever explicit observables and
tolerances exist. Domain-specific diagnostic decompositions—such as the imaging Triad [ 22]—
may be layered on top of this architecture, but the general framework does not require any one
domain-specific diagnostic grammar.
This trust-kernel design suggests a natural extension path. The specification format can decom-
pose into a universal core (the six-tuple), domain-specific extensions (additional Judge gates),
and per-run bindings (concrete dataset, scanner, or benchmark case)—enabling composable
layers rather than monolithic per-domain specifications. Similarly, the 12 general computational
primitives (Table 3) and domain-specific physics vocabularies (e.g., the 11 imaging primitives [ 22])
can coexist as complementary namespaces with versioned mappings. We explore this layered
architecture—including graduated trust tiers, versioned primitive registries, and an open-core
sustainability model—in a companion design document [ 22]. These extensions are design pro-
posals, not validated components of the current system; the empirical claims of this paper rest
entirely on the Judge,S, and the benchmark results reported above.
From scientific domains to explicit, executable, certifiable objects
The trust-kernel design above implies a concrete recipe for how a scientific domain becomes
compatible with the framework. We distinguish three stages:
Stage 1: Explicit.A domain’s tasks becomeexplicitwhen each can be encoded as a finite
spec.md six-tuple(Ω ,E,B,I,O,ε ): a domainΩ, governing equations or operators E, constraints
B, initial or baseline state I, observablesO, and target tolerance ε. This encoding makes the
problem machine-readable and self-contained—independent of any particular solver, platform, or

analyst.
Stage 2: Executable.A domain becomesexecutablewhen at least one solver, workflow, or
deterministic computation pipeline can consume a spec.md and produce outputs in the declared
observable space O. Simulation is sufficient but not necessary: Emay be PDEs and inverse
operators (as in the 12 benchmark domains), but equally it may be metric extraction functions
and validation logic (as in the CT quality-control example above, where no forward or inverse
simulation occurs).
Stage 3: Certifiable.A domain becomescertifiablewhen pre-execution checks establish that

invariants, and the system emits a certificate tied to those acceptance criteria. Domain-specific
diagnostic decompositions—such as the imaging Triad [ 22]—may sit on top of this universal
layer ( spec.md +Judge+certificate), but the general architecture does not require any one
domain-specific diagnostic grammar.
This recipe applies to domains whose tasks can be rendered as deterministic or auditable
computation pipelines with explicit observables and tolerances. The CT QC example shows
that such domains need not involve simulation at all; the 12 benchmark domains show that it
works for simulation-heavy disciplines as well. Once a domain reaches Stage 3, its tasks become
reusable at scale: archived spec.md files can be consumed by multiple independent pipelines,
enabling replay, independent replication, and longitudinal comparison—properties that connect
directly to the reproducibility goals motivating this work.

from 12 external scientists yields 89% success (95% CI: [80%, 95%]) with automated error bounds,

Formal framework
The simulability class S(Definition 1) formalizes the intuition that automated bounded-error
simulation is possible when a problem can be finitely specified (S1), has a unique stable solution
(S2), admits a convergent discretization (S3), and its error can be certified (S4) [ 20]. The
definition is implementation-independent: it does not depend on any particular set of primitives
or discretization strategy. The Judge Agent’s pre-execution gates map onto these conditions:
•Gate 1(dimensional consistency) andGate 4(problem classification) verifyS1: the spec.md
correctly encodes a well-defined problem.
•Gate 2(boundary/initial condition compatibility) verifiesS2: the problem data is complete
and consistent for well-posedness.
•Gate 3(well-posedness: coercivity, CFL, Lipschitz bounds) verifiesS2andS3: the solution
exists uniquely and the chosen discretization converges.
•Gate 5(cost estimation) verifies computational feasibility: the resolution needed to achieve
the target toleranceε(S4) is tractable.
The post-execution quality audit realizes S4 in practice: it computes residuals, checks conservation
laws, and verifies physical bounds, producing the certificate that the approximation meets the
specified tolerance.
Operational run-gates.The reference implementation (PWM [ 22]) distinguishes operational
run-gatesR1–R4 from the formal S-conditions. R1 (spec completeness) proxies S1; R2 (repro-
ducibility) is a necessary condition for S2; R3 (metric integrity) guards the reporting channel for
S3; R4 (budget compliance) guards against runaway computation related to S4. Both families
must pass for a result to be certified: the S-conditions establish mathematical admissibility, while
the R-gates enforce engineering discipline at execution time.
The boundary ∂Sin problem-parameter space is defined as the regime where at least one of
S1–S4 transitions from satisfied to violated. Near ∂S, S4 (certifiability) typically fails first: the
Lipschitz constant grows as L∼|θ−θ c|−αnear a bifurcation parameter θc, making the error
bound vacuous. The Judge’s current checks verify S1–S4 pointwise at the given parameters; they

a certificate (trust verdict with tier). The authoritative representations are the typed objects;

Bifurcation-sensitive rejection heuristics
The residual 1.5% failure rate (2/134 cases) is concentrated at the scientific event horizon—
bifurcation points where S4 (certifiability) fails because the error bound diverges. We propose

three heuristics to detect event-horizon proximity and convert silent failures into flagged cases:
(1) Parameter continuation.After computing a solution ˆxat parameters θ, perturbθ→θ±δ
(defaultδ= 5%) and re-solve. If ∥ˆx(θ+δ)−ˆx(θ)∥/∥ˆx(θ)∥>τcont(proposedτcont= 0.5), flag
the solution as potentially near∂S. This directly probes whetherL DAGis growing.
(2) Lyapunov exponent estimation.Linearize the governing equations at the computed
solution and estimate the largest Lyapunov exponent λ1. Ifλ1>0, the solution is sensitive to
perturbations and S4 (certifiability) may fail. For PDEs, this requires computing the leading
eigenvalue of the linearized operator via Arnoldi iteration.
(3) Ensemble perturbation.Run N(proposedN= 5) perturbed initial/boundary conditions
with perturbation magnitude ϵ(proposedϵ= 10−3). If the coefficient of variation across ensemble
members exceedsτ ens= 0.1, flag. This is a model-free probe of sensitivity.

two known event-horizon failures (Euler buckling symmetry-breaking, critical-Reynolds branch
selection) and measuring the false-positive rate on the 132 interior- Scases is required before
deployment. We report them as a concrete proposal, not a completed solution.

S3 (approximability), and S4 (certifiability). Outside S—at and beyond the scientific event
horizon—four fundamental obstructions prevent any computational system (human or automated)
from guaranteeing bounded-error solutions. Each obstruction maps to the failure of a specific S
condition.

Obstruction 2: Real uncomputability(Blum–Shub–Smale). Decision problems over R
requiring infinite-precision predicates. Example: Mandelbrot set membership for general c∈C
requires determining whether an orbit remains bounded, which is BSS-undecidable for boundary
points. These problems violateS3: no convergent discretization exists at the decision boundary.
Obstruction 3: Quantum measurement irreducibility. Individual measurement outcomes
governed by the Born rule. Only probability distributions—not individual realizations—are
computable. Example: “Which detector clicks in a Stern–Gerlach experiment?” is inherently
stochastic. Note: thedistributionof outcomes is in S(via Monte Carlo sampling). This
obstruction violatesS2(Hadamard stability): the individual-outcome “problem” is not well-
posed (no unique solution exists).

numbers such as Chaitin’sΩ(the halting probability of a universal Turing machine). No finite
computation can approximateΩto arbitrary precision. This violatesS4(certifiability): no
computable error bound can be produced, even though finite approximations may exist.
Whether these four obstructions are theonlybarriers to membership in Sis stated as Conjecture 1
in the main text (Obstruction Completeness). The non-trivial direction—that every problem
outside Sfails due to one of these four—is an open question connecting AI-assisted simulation
to the foundations of computable analysis.

practice, the scientific event horizon is encountered throughnear-violationsof Sconditions—

S8.1 Formal grammar
A valid spec.md file is a structured Markdown document whose abstract syntax is defined by
the following context-free grammar (in EBNF notation):
spec_file = header , domain , equations , boundary , initial ,
observables , tolerance , { extension } ;
header = "# Specification:" , TITLE , NEWLINE ;
domain = "## Domain" , NEWLINE , { key_value } ;
equations = "## Equations" , NEWLINE , { equation_block | key_value } ;
boundary = "## Boundary Conditions" , NEWLINE , { key_value } ;
initial = "## Initial Conditions" , NEWLINE , { key_value } ;
observables = "## Observables" , NEWLINE , { key_value } ;
tolerance = "## Tolerance" , NEWLINE , { key_value } ;
extension = "## " , SECTION_NAME , NEWLINE , { key_value } ;
key_value = KEY , ":" , VALUE , NEWLINE ;
equation_block = KEY , ":" , "|" , NEWLINE , { INDENTED_LINE } ;
KEY = /[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*/ ;
VALUE = /[^\n]+/ ;
TITLE = /[^\n]+/ ;
The six mandatory sections map one-to-one to the S1 six-tuple:
•## Domain→Ω(computational domain)
35

•## Equations→E(governing equations)
•## Boundary Conditions→B(boundary conditions)
•## Initial Conditions→I(initial conditions)
•## Observables→O(output functional)
•## Tolerance→ε(target tolerance)
Additional sections (e.g., ## Primitives Required ,## Task Instance Variations ) are per-
mitted as extensions but are not required for Smembership. Key-value pairs within each section
use YAML-compatible syntax for machine parseability while remaining human-readable.
Aspec.md file isvalidif and only if: (1) all six mandatory sections are present with at least one
non-empty key-value pair; (2) theTolerancesection contains at least one numerical threshold;
(3) the Equations section contains at least one mathematical expression (in plain text, LaTeX,
or symbolic form). Validation is implemented as a 12-line Python function in the pipeline (see
validate_specmd.pyin the repository).
S8.2 External tool adapters (preliminary)
To demonstrate that spec.md is not locked to our pipeline, we have developed preliminary
adapters that translate a subset ofspec.mdfiles into input formats for two external tools:
FEniCS adapter.For spec.md files describing linear elliptic PDEs (Poisson, heat equation,
linear elasticity), a Python script parses the six-tuple and generates a FEniCS variational form
(.pyfile). Tested on Poisson ( ∇2u=fon[0,1]2) and heat equation ( ∂tu=κ∇2u); both produce
solutions matching the pipeline output to machine precision. The adapter handles: domain
geometry (rectangular, from the Domain section), Dirichlet/Neumann BCs (from Boundary
Conditions), initial conditions (from Initial Conditions), and target tolerance (from Tolerance,
mappedtomeshrefinement). Itdoesnotyethandlenon-rectangulardomains, nonlinearequations,
or coupled systems.
COMSOL adapter.For the same linear elliptic subset, a script generates COMSOL .mph
parameter files via the COMSOL–MATLAB LiveLink API. Tested on Poisson only; the generated
COMSOL model produces results within10−6of the pipeline output. This adapter is more
limited than the FEniCS adapter and requires a COMSOL license.
These adapters are proof-of-concept demonstrations covering <5%of the problems in S.
Extending them to nonlinear, time-dependent, and coupled problems is a significant engineering
effort. We include them to make the universality aspiration concrete, not to claim current
universality.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
This document introduces a "Judge Agent" designed to improve the reliability of AI-generated scientific simulation code. The main points covered are:

*   **Problem:** AI-generated simulation code often fails silently on non-textbook problems, leading to incorrect results that appear plausible.
*   **Solution:** A "Judge Agent" automates classical mathematical validation techniques (well-posedness, convergence, error certification) to detect these silent failures.
*   **Methodology:**
    *   **Simulability Class S:** A formal framework defining problems that can be solved reliably with bounded error, based on finite specifiability, Hadamard stability, approximability, and certifiability.
    *   **spec.md:** A structured, machine-readable format for specifying scientific computation problems, making them solver-independent.
    *   **Three-Agent Pipeline:** A system comprising a Plan Agent (natural language to spec.md), a Judge Agent (validation), and an Execute Agent (solver).
*   **Results:**
    *   The Judge Agent reduces the silent-failure rate from 42% to 1.5% across 134 test cases in 12 scientific domains.
    *   A prospective benchmark with 72 blinded tasks from independent scientists showed an 89% success rate with the Judge, compared to 53% without it.
    *   In a powered experiment on clinical CT reconstruction (n=200), the pipeline achieved 99% of expert quality.
*   **Limitations and Future Work:**
    *   A residual 1.5% failure rate occurs at "bifurcation points" where certifiability breaks down.
    *   Proposed heuristics to detect these boundary cases are under development.
    *   The system is not intended to replace specialized solvers for well-defined problems but serves as a validated first-answer system for AI-generated code.
*   **Broader Impact:** The `spec.md` format and validation framework are proposed to extend beyond simulation to measurement-validation pipelines and to address the reproducibility crisis.

nodes.title: The simulability class and its boundary
nodes.summary:
The provided document describes a formal specification format called `spec.md` for scientific computation problems. This format uses a YAML-compatible syntax within Markdown and is structured into six mandatory sections and two optional sections.

The six mandatory sections define the "S1 six-tuple" which encapsulates a problem:
*   **Domain (Ω):** Describes the geometry, dimension, and grid of the computational space.
*   **Equations (E):** Specifies the governing partial differential equations (PDEs) or operators, along with their parameters.
*   **Boundary Conditions (B):** Details the constraints on the solution at the domain boundaries, such as Dirichlet or Neumann conditions.
*   **Initial Conditions (I):** Defines the starting state for time-dependent problems or an initial guess for iterative solvers.
*   **Observables (O):** Lists the output quantities to be computed, including their units.
*   **Tolerance (ε):** Sets the numerical thresholds and the metric used to determine success.

The two optional sections are:
*   **Primitives Required:** Links to a basis of fundamental computational primitives.
*   **Task Instance Variations:** Defines splits for public, development, and hidden test sets.

The document also introduces the concept of the "simulability class S," which defines problems that can be solved with bounded error by an automated pipeline. This class requires:
*   **Finite Specifiability:** The problem can be represented by the finite `spec.md` tuple.
*   **Hadamard Stability:** The mapping from problem data to solution is well-posed.
*   **Approximability:** A convergent discretization scheme exists.
*   **Certifiability:** A computable procedure exists to verify the approximation's accuracy against a given tolerance.

The document highlights the importance of the "Judge Agent" in verifying these conditions, particularly certifiability (S4), which distinguishes problems that are merely computable from those that are certifiably accurate. The "boundary ∂S" represents the regime where at least one of these conditions fails, posing fundamental limits on automated simulation guarantees. The document presents evidence showing that the Judge Agent significantly improves the success rate of automated pipelines, especially for more difficult and frontier problems.

nodes.title: Why not a human analyst?
nodes.summary:

*   **Beyond Simulation:** The spec.md format and the underlying six-tuple structure of S are shown to be applicable to measurement-validation pipelines, not just simulations. A detailed example of automated CT quality control (QC) is provided, mapping the six-tuple components to QC workflow elements.
*   **Comparison to Human Analysts:** While a formal comparison is lacking, the paper estimates that manual verification of the mathematical checks performed by the Judge Agent would be significantly more time-consuming.
*   **Validated First-Answer System:** The Judge Agent is presented as a tool for providing validated first answers, especially for researchers lacking numerical expertise or when the alternative is unvalidated AI-generated code. Simulation is not a prerequisite; deterministic measurement-validation pipelines are sufficient.
*   **Layered Architecture and Composability:** The specification format is designed to be decomposable into a universal core, domain-specific extensions, and per-run bindings, enabling composable layers. Similarly, computational primitives can coexist with domain-specific vocabularies.

nodes.title: Not better, but validated

*   **Reliability and Cost:** Manual verification (S1-S4) is time-consuming (2-4 hours per problem) but achieves comparable reliability to automated checks, albeit at a higher cost. A formal human-analyst comparison is planned.
*   **Intellectual Novelty:** The core innovation lies in formalizing "certifiability" (S4) as a distinct requirement from mere computability. A problem can be solvable without being provably accurate. While specialized solvers (COMSOL, FEniCS) offer higher accuracy on single PDEs, the described pipeline serves as a validated "first-answer" system for researchers lacking numerical expertise, offering an alternative to unvalidated LLM-generated code.
*   **Limitations:** The system has a 1.5% failure rate, primarily near bifurcation points (∂S) where certifiability fails due to diverging error bounds. The system cannot distinguish between solution branches without global landscape information. Proposed rejection heuristics are not yet validated, meaning the pipeline carries a small risk of undetected qualitative errors near ∂S.
*   **Design Implications (Trust Kernel):** The system's components (six-tuple, S1-S4 verification, audit record) form a "minimal trust kernel." This kernel allows new scientific domains to integrate by providing benchmarkable tasks representable in a finite specification format, at least one executable realization, and a post-execution certificate. Deterministic measurement-validation pipelines are sufficient where observables and tolerances exist.
*   **Extensibility and Layered Architecture:** The design supports composable layers, with a universal core specification, domain-specific extensions, and per-run bindings. Computational primitives and domain-specific vocabularies can coexist as complementary namespaces. This layered architecture, including graduated trust tiers and versioned registries, is detailed in a companion document.
*   **Scientific Domain Compatibility:** The framework requires domains to become "explicit, executable, and certifiable." This involves encoding tasks into a machine-readable six-tuple specification (Ω, E, B, I, O, ε).

nodes.title: What is established, what is not, and the main open problem
nodes.summary:
The partial document describes a three-stage framework for making computational domains "executable" and "certifiable." Stage 2, "Executable," is achieved when a domain can produce outputs within a declared observable space using solvers, workflows, or deterministic computation pipelines, which may or may not involve simulation. Stage 3, "Certifiable," adds pre-execution checks (S1-S4 verification by a "Judge") and post-execution audits to ensure outputs meet declared tolerances and invariants, resulting in a system-emitted certificate. This framework is applicable to domains with deterministic or auditable computation pipelines and explicit observables and tolerances, and it enables reusable tasks, replay, replication, and longitudinal comparison.

The document then outlines what has been established and what remains unestablished regarding this framework. Established points include significant reductions in silent failures through automated verification, improved success rates on blinded tasks with automated error bounds, high quality in clinical CT applications, the applicability of the specification format beyond simulation, and the coverage of computational primitives.

Unestablished points include the reliability of the specification encoding generated by LLMs, uneven statistical rigor across different domains, the completeness of the computational primitives for all convergent discretizations, the robustness of the pipeline to LLM version changes, the adoption of the specification format as a community standard, and the lack of formal comparison with human analysts.

nodes.title: The main open problem: the residual 1.5%

These failures occur at bifurcation points where the certifiability condition (S4) breaks down due to diverging error bounds. The current system checks conditions S1-S4 pointwise but cannot detect proximity to the boundary of these conditions without global landscape information. The document proposes three detection heuristics that are not yet implemented or validated. The adversarial boundary suite is deemed too small for reliable statistics, and a larger suite is recommended.

The document also addresses a conflict of interest due to the single-author nature of the paper from a company developing the platform. Mitigations include an independent coordinator, external scientists for task evaluation, replication by independent researchers, and public archiving of all code and data.

The "Methods" section details the formal framework for simulability (S1-S4) and how the "Judge's" pre-execution gates map to these conditions. It also describes operational run-gates (R1-R4) that enforce engineering discipline during execution. The boundary of the problem-parameter space (∂S) is defined as the regime where at least one of S1-S4 is violated, with S4 typically failing first near bifurcation parameters.

This partial document describes a framework for defining and verifying computational problems. It outlines six key components of a "specification tuple" (S) that makes problems machine-readable and self-contained:

*   **Computational domain (Ω):** Defines the geometric and topological space where the problem is posed, including dimensionality, coordinate system, discretization, and length scales.
*   **Governing equations (E):** Specifies the mathematical model relating unknowns to data, including PDEs, integral equations, or algebraic systems, along with all physical parameters and their values.
*   **Boundary conditions (B):** Details the constraints on the solution at the domain's boundary or interfaces, including type and values.
*   **Initial conditions (I):** Describes the starting state for time-dependent problems or the initial guess for iterative solvers.
*   **Observables (O):** Defines the output functionals or derived quantities to be computed from the solution, specifying the form and acceptance criteria.
*   **Target tolerance (ε):** Sets the quantitative accuracy threshold for success, stated with respect to a named metric and a reference.

The document also highlights three crucial properties for computational problems:

*   **Computable modulus of continuity (S1):** Implies that the solution has a well-defined continuity property that can be computed.
*   **Approximability (S3):** Guarantees the existence of a convergent discretization scheme that can approximate the solution with a computable convergence rate.
*   **Certifiability (S4):** Ensures the existence of a computable procedure to produce a verified upper bound on the approximation error, proving its accuracy within a given tolerance.

The document emphasizes that certifiability (S4) is a key distinction, separating problems that can be approximated from those whose approximations can be rigorously proven to be good enough. This distinction necessitates a "Judge Agent" for automated verification. The Judge Agent performs pre-execution checks for S1-S4 and a post-execution audit to ensure physical invariants are met.

nodes.title: The boundary ∂S
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses a framework for automated scientific simulation that aims to provide certifiable solutions. The main points covered are:

*   **The "Scientific Event Horizon" ($\partial S$):** This boundary represents a fundamental limit on certifiable simulation, where conditions for well-posedness (S2) or certifiability (S4) degrade, leading to pipeline failures. Problems near this boundary, such as symmetry-breaking or branch selection near critical parameters, are where most failures occur.

*   **The Judge Agent's Role:** The Judge Agent is introduced as a mechanism to close the "reliability gap." It verifies membership in a set of conditions (S1-S4) that define a certifiable simulation.

*   **Impact of the Judge Agent on Success Rates:**
    *   Without the Judge, the pipeline produces wrong answers on a significant percentage of problems (42% on development, 47% on prospective tasks), particularly on difficult, non-textbook problems near $\partial S$.
    *   With the Judge verifying S1-S4, the success rate dramatically improves to 100% on development problems and 89% on held-out tasks, with automated error bounds provided for successful solutions.

*   **Difficulty Stratification:** Problems are categorized into four tiers based on their proximity to $\partial S$: Development (Dev), Textbook, Standard, and Frontier. The success rate of the pipeline without the Judge agent drops significantly as problems move from Textbook to Frontier tiers, highlighting the Judge's importance for more challenging tasks.

*   **Case Studies and Validation:**
    *   **Clinical CT Reconstruction:** A powered validation using real clinical CT sinograms demonstrates the framework's effectiveness, achieving 99% of expert quality with a significant setup-time efficiency gain. Figure 4 visually illustrates the improvement with and without the Judge.
    *   **Seismic Full-Waveform Inversion and Combustion:** These are presented as case studies, showcasing the framework's ability to handle complex problems and achieve high quality with substantial setup-time efficiency compared to expert workflows.
    *   **Setup-Time Efficiency ($\rho$):** The framework offers a substantial efficiency gain in setup time (problem formulation, method selection, parameter tuning, validation) rather than compute time, with a median efficiency ratio of 480x across 12 validated domains.

*   **Prospective Benchmark (72 Tasks):** A blinded challenge involving external scientists demonstrates the framework's performance on real-world research problems. The Judge Agent correctly identified and rejected ill-posed problems, and the overall success rate was high.

*   **Failure Analysis:**
    *   The document details a failure analysis across 134 test cases, showing how S-verification reduces silent failures in stages: pre-execution gates (42% to 6%) and a post-execution quality audit (6% to 1.5%).
    *   The residual 1.5% failures occur at bifurcation points near $\partial S$, where certifiability (S4) breaks down due to diverging error bounds. This is identified as the paper's main open problem, with proposed heuristics for improvement.
    *   Ablation studies show the importance of individual verification gates, particularly the well-posedness gate.

*   **Computational Cost:** The Judge Agent's overhead is a small percentage of the total wall-clock time, with the primary value proposition being setup-time efficiency.

structure.title: Specification: {Title} header
structure.summary:
This document excerpt discusses a method for bounding and certifying the error in computations performed on a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). The main points covered are:

*   **Error Bound Derivation:** It presents an inductive derivation of an error bound ($\epsilon_{total}$) for a general DAG, relating it to the error at individual nodes ($\epsilon_i$) and an "effective amplification factor" ($\ell_i$).
*   **Certifiability Assumption:** It highlights the importance of the certifiability assumption (A4/S4), which bounds the amplification factors and allows for a cruder error bound.
*   **Resolution Selection:** It details how to select resolution parameters ($\epsilon_i$) for each node to achieve a desired total error ($\epsilon$), ensuring these parameters are achievable given problem-specific constants ($C_i, q_i$).
*   **Computational Cost:** It establishes that the total computational cost ($T_{comp}$) is finite if individual primitive costs ($T_i$) are finite for positive resolution parameters.
*   **Agent Roles:** It connects the error bounding and resolution selection process to the roles of different agents:
    *   **Judge Agent:** Verifies assumptions (S1-S3) through pre-execution gates, ensuring dimensional consistency, problem classification, data completeness, well-posedness, and cost feasibility.
    *   **Execute Agent (AE):** Sets resolution parameters and performs a post-execution quality audit to certify the result (S4).
*   **Intellectual Novelty:** The authors emphasize that their contribution lies in the formalization and automation of certifiability as a computability requirement, rather than novel mathematical discoveries.
*   **Bound Breakdown:** It identifies the "scientific event horizon" (boundary of the problem domain) as a point where certifiability fails, leading to infinite amplification factors, vanishing resolution parameters, and infinite computational cost, rendering the error bound vacuous.

*   **Proposition S5: Automated Bounded-Error Realizability within S:** This proposition outlines the conditions under which a three-agent pipeline (Plan Agent, Judge Agent, and implicitly a simulation execution agent) can produce a simulation result with a guaranteed error bound.
*   **Assumptions (S1-S4):** The proposition relies on four key assumptions:
    *   **Finite Specifiability (S1):** The problem can be finitely represented and validated by the Judge Agent.
    *   **Hadamard Stability (S2):** The underlying mathematical operators are well-posed with finite Lipschitz constants.
    *   **Approximability (S3):** Discretizations of subproblems are convergent with bounded errors.
    *   **Certifiability (S4):** The composition of subproblems in a computational Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) has a bounded Lipschitz constant, enabling error bound computation.
*   **Proof Outline:** The proof is presented in three steps:
    *   **Step 1 (Finite Specification):** Details how the Plan Agent generates a specification file and the Judge Agent verifies its adherence to the simulability class S. It also describes the pipeline's behavior upon rejection by the Judge Agent.
    *   **Step 2 (DAG Decomposition):** Explains how the problem is decomposed into a DAG of primitive operations, referencing a "Primitive Realizability proposition" and defining DAG size and depth. It reiterates the Lipschitz constants and discretization errors for each primitive.
    *   **Step 3 (Error Propagation):** Demonstrates how errors propagate through the DAG, using induction and providing an example for a chain of two primitives to illustrate the error bound calculation.

structure.title: Discussion
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses the "Judge Agent," an automated system for validating AI-generated scientific simulations. The main points covered are:

*   **Effectiveness of the Judge Agent:** The Judge Agent significantly reduces silent failures in AI-generated simulations, decreasing the failure rate from 42% to 1.5%.
*   **The `spec.md` Format:** This format defines what is simulable in practice by providing a concrete, machine-parseable serialization of the simulability class `S`. It aims to address the reproducibility crisis by allowing researchers to share simulation intent independently of specific software.
*   **Portability and Community Adoption of `spec.md`:** While currently used by a single pipeline, the format's potential as a community exchange format is an empirical question dependent on external adoption. Efforts are underway to develop adapters for other platforms like FEniCS and COMSOL.
*   **Extension of `spec.md` Beyond Simulation:** The `spec.md` format, based on the six-tuple `S`, can be extended to non-simulation workflows, such as measurement-validation pipelines.
*   **Application to CT Quality Control (QC):** The document provides a detailed mapping of the `S` six-tuple components to a clinical CT QC workflow, demonstrating the format's versatility for deterministic computation pipelines with defined inputs, outputs, and acceptance criteria.
*   **Rationale for Automation:** The Judge Agent automates mathematical checks (e.g., well-posedness, convergence) that would typically be performed manually by a human analyst. A limitation is noted for not including a formal comparison with human analysts.

structure.title: Why not a human analyst?
structure.summary:

*   **Claim and Evidence:** The paper claims that the Judge Agent significantly reduces the reliability gap in AI-generated scientific simulations. Evidence is presented showing a substantial increase in silent failures when the Judge Agent is removed.
*   **Sand Specification (spec.md):** This format defines what is simulable in practice by providing a concrete, machine-parseable serialization of the simulability class S. It aims to address the reproducibility crisis by allowing researchers to share simulation intent without specific software dependencies. The portability of this format is being tested through adapters to other simulation tools.
*   **Beyond Simulation:** The spec.md format and the underlying six-tuple structure of S are shown to be applicable to measurement-validation pipelines, not just simulations. A detailed example of automated CT quality control (QC) is provided, mapping the six-tuple components to QC workflow elements.
*   **Comparison to Human Analysts:** While a formal comparison is lacking, the paper estimates that manual verification of the mathematical checks performed by the Judge Agent would be significantly more time-consuming.
*   **Validated First-Answer System:** The Judge Agent is presented as a tool for providing validated first answers, especially for researchers lacking numerical expertise or when the alternative is unvalidated AI-generated code. It is acknowledged that the system is not always more accurate than specialized solvers but offers validated reliability.
*   **Open Problem: Residual Failures:** The remaining 1.5% of failures occur at the boundary of the simulability class S, where certifiability breaks down near bifurcation points. The Judge Agent cannot distinguish between simulation branches in these cases, and proposed heuristics are not yet validated.
*   **Design Implications: Trust Kernel:** The six-tuple, Judge's verification, and audit record form a "trust kernel" that allows new scientific domains to integrate by providing benchmarkable tasks, executable realizations, and acceptance criteria. Simulation is not a prerequisite; deterministic measurement-validation pipelines are sufficient.
*   **Layered Architecture and Composability:** The specification format is designed to be decomposable into a universal core, domain-specific extensions, and per-run bindings, enabling composable layers. Similarly, computational primitives can coexist with domain-specific vocabularies.
*   **Stages for Domain Compatibility:** The document outlines a three-stage process for a scientific domain to become compatible with the framework: becoming explicit (encoding tasks in spec.md), executable (having at least one realization), and certifiable (producing a post-execution certificate).

structure.title: Not better, but validated.
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses a system for validating scientific computations, focusing on its reliability, novelty, limitations, and design implications. Key points include:

*   **Reliability and Cost:** Manual verification (S1-S4) is time-consuming (2-4 hours per problem) but achieves comparable reliability to automated checks, albeit at a higher cost. A formal human-analyst comparison is planned.
*   **Intellectual Novelty:** The core innovation lies in formalizing "certifiability" (S4) as a distinct requirement from mere computability. A problem can be solvable without being provably accurate. While specialized solvers (COMSOL, FEniCS) offer higher accuracy on single PDEs, the described pipeline serves as a validated "first-answer" system for researchers lacking numerical expertise, offering an alternative to unvalidated LLM-generated code.
*   **Limitations:** The system has a 1.5% failure rate, primarily near bifurcation points (∂S) where certifiability fails due to diverging error bounds. The system cannot distinguish between solution branches without global landscape information. Proposed rejection heuristics are not yet validated, meaning the pipeline carries a small risk of undetected qualitative errors near ∂S.
*   **Design Implications (Trust Kernel):** The system's components (six-tuple, S1-S4 verification, audit record) form a "minimal trust kernel." This kernel allows new scientific domains to integrate by providing benchmarkable tasks representable in a finite specification format, at least one executable realization, and a post-execution certificate. Deterministic measurement-validation pipelines are sufficient where observables and tolerances exist.
*   **Extensibility and Layered Architecture:** The design supports composable layers, with a universal core specification, domain-specific extensions, and per-run bindings. Computational primitives and domain-specific vocabularies can coexist as complementary namespaces. This layered architecture, including graduated trust tiers and versioned registries, is detailed in a companion document.
*   **Scientific Domain Compatibility:** The framework requires domains to become "explicit, executable, and certifiable." This involves encoding tasks into a machine-readable six-tuple specification (Ω, E, B, I, O, ε).

structure.title: What is established, what is not, and the main open problem
structure.summary:
The partial document describes a three-stage framework for making computational domains "executable" and "certifiable." *   **Certifiability Assumption:** It highlights the importance of the certifiability assumption (A4/S4), which bounds the amplification factors and allows for a cruder error bound.
*   **Resolution Selection:** It details how to select resolution parameters ($\epsilon_i$) for each node to achieve a desired total error ($\epsilon$), ensuring these parameters are achievable given problem-specific constants ($C_i, q_i$).
*   **Computational Cost:** It establishes that the total computational cost ($T_{comp}$) is finite if individual primitive costs ($T_i$) are finite for positive resolution parameters.
*   **Agent Roles:** It connects the error bounding and resolution selection process to the roles of different agents:
    *   **Judge Agent:** Verifies assumptions (S1-S3) through pre-execution gates, ensuring dimensional consistency, problem classification, data completeness, well-posedness, and cost feasibility.

This document excerpt discusses the theoretical framework for automated bounded-error simulation, focusing on the conditions required for a problem to be simulable (within the set S) and the obstructions that arise when problems lie outside this set (at the "scientific event horizon").

The main points covered are:

*   **Error Bounds and Certifiability:** It details how error bounds are derived for general directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of computational tasks, emphasizing the role of "effective amplification factors" and the importance of "certifiability" (S4) as a distinct requirement from "approximability" (S3). The process of setting resolution parameters (hi) to achieve a total error (εtotal) is explained.
*   **Connection to Judge Agent Gates:** The document maps the assumptions required for error bounds (S1-S4) to the pre-execution gates of a "Judge Agent," illustrating how these gates verify problem well-definedness, consistency, well-posedness, and computational feasibility. The post-execution quality audit is linked to realizing S4 in practice.
*   **Novelty and Automation:** The authors highlight that their contribution is the formalization and automation of classical verification techniques, rather than introducing new mathematical concepts for error bounds.
*   **The Scientific Event Horizon:** This section defines the boundary beyond which guaranteed bounded-error solutions are impossible. It identifies four fundamental obstructions that prevent problems from being in the simulable class S:
    1.  **Logical Undecidability (Gödel–Turing):** Violates S3 (approximability) due to problems reducible to the halting problem.
    2.  **Real Uncomputability (Blum–Shub–Smale):** Violates S3 (approximability) for decision problems over R requiring infinite-precision predicates.
    3.  **Quantum Measurement Irreducibility:** Violates S2 (Hadamard stability) as individual quantum measurement outcomes are not uniquely determined.
    4.  **Infinite-Precision Barriers:** Violates S4 (certifiability) when solutions depend on non-computable real numbers, making error bounds uncomputable.
*   **Practical Implications:** While obstructions are theoretical, the scientific event horizon is practically encountered through near-violations of S conditions, particularly S4 near bifurcation points where error bounds diverge. Current Judge Agent gates detect exact violations but not proximity to this horizon.
*   **Domain Validations:** The document lists seven additional domains (epidemiology, granular flow, electromagnetics, quantum chemistry, fluid dynamics, structural mechanics, optics) where the simulation pipeline was validated, all confirmed to be within the simulable set S.
*   **Primitive Basis and Realizability:** It discusses a concrete basis of 12 computational primitives that can realize S3 and S4 for problems discretized using standard numerical methods. Witness problems are provided to demonstrate the necessity of each primitive.

structure.title: Initial Conditions
structure.summary:
This partial document describes a system for generating and verifying scientific simulation specifications, likely for use with Large Language Models (LLMs). The main points covered are:

*   **Adversarial Testing of LLM-Generated Specifications:** A comprehensive list of 50 adversarial test inputs (Table S13) is presented, categorized into three types:
    *   **Ambiguous/incomplete inputs:** These test the LLM's ability to handle underspecified problems, requiring redesign or human clarification.
    *   **Subtle S-boundary issues:** These probe the LLM's performance near the boundaries of its capabilities, testing for issues like missing initial conditions, near-singularities, and extreme parameter ratios.
    *   **Event-horizon probes:** These focus on cases where the LLM might produce a numerically correct solution (L2 correct) but one that is qualitatively wrong, often missed by automated audits.

*   **LLM Backbone Sensitivity:** The performance of the specification generation component (AP) is evaluated across different LLM backbones (Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Claude-3-Opus, GPT-4-Turbo) on 12 development problems (Table S14). The results indicate that while most backbones perform well, there can be specific failures (e.g., GPT-4-Turbo's failure on GRI-Mech ignition delay).

*   **Fragility and Verification:** The document highlights the potential fragility of LLM performance with updates and emphasizes the role of the S-verification gates (S1-S4) as a safety net to reject invalid specifications. It recommends pinning model versions for production.

*   **Effectiveness of S-Verification:** Extensive comparisons (Table S15) show a significant drop in success rate when S-verification (AJ) is removed, particularly for more difficult "frontier" problems. This underscores the critical role of the verification system.

*   **Ablation Study of Verification Gates:** An ablation study (Table S16) analyzes the contribution of individual verification gates (well-posedness, BC/IC compatibility, dimensional consistency, classification, cost estimation, quality audit) to the overall success rate. The well-posedness gate (S2+S3) is identified as the most critical, and the quality audit (S4) is important for catching qualitative failures.

*   **Performance Metrics and Distributions:** Supplementary figures present distributions of performance metrics like PSNR (Figure S1) and quality ratios (Figure S2) for different task types.

*   **Scalability and Overhead:** The scalability of the system is discussed, including the wall-clock time breakdown for different components (AP, AJ, AE) and the overhead of the S-verification process (Figure S3). The verification overhead is shown to be relatively constant, decreasing as a proportion of total time with increasing problem size.

*   **Formal Grammar for Specifications:** A formal context-free grammar (EBNF notation) is provided for the `spec.md` file format, defining its structure and mandatory sections that map to the S1 six-tuple (domain, equations, boundary conditions, initial conditions, observables, tolerance).

The supplementary figures (S1, S2, S3) present quantitative results and analyses related to a framework's performance. Figure S1 compares the per-case Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) distribution for CT reconstruction between the framework and an expert baseline, indicating a slightly left-shifted distribution for the framework with comparable spread. It outlines the mandatory sections (header, domain, equations, boundary, initial, observables, tolerance) and their mapping to a six-tuple representation. It also specifies rules for key-value pairs, equation blocks, and the validation criteria for a `spec.md` file.

The external tool adapters section (S8.2) describes preliminary adapters developed to translate `spec.md` files into input formats for external tools like FEniCS and COMSOL. These adapters are presented as proof-of-concept demonstrations for a subset of linear elliptic PDEs, showcasing the potential for interoperability with existing simulation software. The limitations and ongoing engineering efforts for extending these adapters are also mentioned.
